spans.content: Temperature as a Pitting Criterion*
R. J. BRIGHAM and E. W. TOZER*
Abstract
On the basis of three independent test methods, two potentiostatically controlled and one freely
corroding, temperature has been shown quantitatively to be an important criterion for describing the
onset of pitting corrosion in molybdenum containing austenitic stainless steels. The temperature at
which pitting is initiated in acid chloride solution has been related to the|molybdenum content of the
alloys.
In an earlier presentation,1 the pitting characteristics of a
series of molybdenum containing austenitic stainless steels
were presented as a function of potential and temperature.
These data, reproduced in Figure 1, are characterized by an
intermediate, strongly temperature dependent, potential
range which is bracketed at lower and higher potentials by
plateaus which are insensitive to temperature changes. The
upper plateau has been shown to result from the onset of
transpassivity.
It is only in the intermediate potential range that the
relative pitting resistance of the series of alloys can be
distinguished, and in Figure 1 it is the relative position of
each of the curves with respect to the temperature axis that
makes possible a ranking of the alloys. Because the curves
for each of the different alloys collectively make up a
family, the determination of a single point in the inter-
mediate potential range for each alloy would be indicative
of the whole curve for that alloy and consequently define
the relative resistance of each of the alloys.
A simplified screening test, therefore appears to be
available in which, at a fixed potential in the intermediate
range, the temperature of the solution is increased until
pitting is observed. This technique would appear to take
advantage of the fact that an intermediate potential, such as
+500 mV (SCE), is common to all of the alloys regardless
of their relative resistances with respect to temperature and
the steep slope of the temperature-potential curves would
suggest a well defined transition.

Effect of Testing Rate
The two testing techniques compared above (increasing
potential at fixed temperature and increasing temperature
at fixed potential) and found to correlate very well are
based on relatively short term tests. Although it appears
that they can be used effectively as a screening test to rank
the pitting susceptibility of a series of alloys, the signifi-
cance of these data with respect to long term exposure is
not immediately clear. Leckie and
\mathrm { U h l i g } ^ { \bar { 2 } }
have shown, for
increasing potential runs at fixed temperature, that the
values of critical pitting potential are rate dependent, being
more noble at high scan rates for potentials in the general
area corresponding to the lower plateau of Figure 1.
However, Bond and
\mathbf { L i z l o v s } ^ { 3 }
found the potential for pitting
to be more active at high scan rates, but these results were
obtained at generally more noble potentials which would
correspond to the potential region near the upper plateau in
Figure 1. On the basis of these observations, extrapolation
of the curves of Figure 1 to infinitely slow scan rates would
result in an overall increase in slope toward the vertical in
the intermediate potential range, brought about by further
increases in high potential values and decreases in low
values. No lateral shift with respect to temperature would
be expected in the intermediate potential range, nor are the
upper plateau pótential values expected to change appre-
ciably in describing infinitely slow scan rates (long exposure
times). The lower plateau potential values will, of course,
decrease with decreasing scan rate as shown by Leckie and
Uhlig.2
Shape changes in Figure 1 of the type proposed above
would indicate that long term pitting tests should be
insensitive to potential over the whole intermediate poten-
tial range, but very dependent upon test temperature. Data
produced at +500 mV (SCE) is apparently near the
postulated point of rotation of the transition section of the
curves and should therefore be applicable in predicting long
term pitting behavior. To some extent this hypothesis is
substantiated by the data of Figure 2 which correlate as
well for the less resistant alloys (short exposure times) as
for the more resistant alloys (exposure times approaching
one hour). Further corroboration was obtained by means of
a series of longer exposures carried out as a function of
temperature in a solution with oxidizing power in the
intermediate potential range.

\mathbb { L i z l o v s } , { \mathbf 3 }

Discussion
The results of the FeCl3 exposure tests (Table 3) agree
with the
\mathrm { T } _ { 5 0 0 }
values (Table 2) obtained for the same alloys
in a solution of similar chloride activity and pH, and the
\mathrm { T } _ { 5 0 0 }
values were shown to correlate with the earlier data
(Figure 2). It could be argued that this agreement between
shorter and longer term tests, one potentiostatically con-
trolled and the other freely corroding, is fortuitous.
However, such an agreement is to be expected if the pitting
curves in the intermediate potential range of Figure 1
approach the vertical for infinitely slow scan rates as
postulated above.
Experimental confirmation of the proposed vertical
temperature-potential curves in the intermediate potential
region to describe infinitely slow scan rates was obtained by
a series of 66 hour exposure experiments. Samples of 317L
stainless steel were exposed to the following solutions of
similar chloride activities but very different oxidizing
power: 16% sodium hypochlorite (domestic bleach) con-
taining 3.5% NaCl, 10% FeCl3, and 5% potassium ferricya-
nide containing 3.5% NaCl. In all cases, pitting was
observed at a temperature of 30 C or higher, but not at à
temperature of 27.5 C or lower. The strong dependence on
temperature and not on potential suggests that there exists
for each wholly austenitic steel a critical pitting tempera-
ture below which the steel will not pit regardless of
potential and exposure time. The data presented here are
considered to approximate such a parameter.
In Figure 3, this critical pitting temperature, within the
limits of accuracy of the techniques described here, is
plotted as a function of the Mo content of the various
steels, both experimental and commercial. In the case of
FeCl3 exposure tests, the low temperature end of the error
bars plotted in Figure 3 represents the temperature at and
below which pitting was not observed, while the high
temperature end indicates the temperature at and above

which pitting was observed after a 24 hour exposure. The
minimum and maximum Tsoo values are also plotted in
Figure 3 as error bars. In each case, these bars represent the
degree of uncertainty in determining the critical pitting
temperature by these techniques. The average pitting
behavior of all the steels in the composition range 3 to 7.5%
Mo can be described by the empirical equation

Although the critical pitting temperature of a steel has
been obtained in three different but apparently equivalent
ways, the preferred method appears to be by the use of
FeCl3 exposures. This technique minimizes testing rate
effects, differentiates between pitting and crevice and end
grain attack, uses samples of any geometry, and requires a
minimum of electronic gadgetry. Regardless of the tech-
nique used, however, the correlation shown in Figure 3
appears to be a valid and workable way of describing the
pitting susceptibility of wholly austenitic alloys in terms of
a parameter with design significance.

Conclusions
The pitting characteristics of molybdenum containing
austenitic stainless steel, produced in both experimental 50
pound heats and on a commercial scale, have been
described by a single parameter, the critical pitting tempera-
ture, which depends in a regular way on the Mo content of
the steel. However, these data are valid only for pit
nucleation on a flat surface. Preliminary results indicate that
these temperature values should be reduced considerably to
describe the onset of edge or crevice attack, which
consequently appear to constitute a more likely mode of
service failure than pitting. This area is presently under
investigation.
